questions.question: What did Lencho hope for?
answer_steps: He hoped for rain, a downpour or at least a shower.
His field of ripe corn needed rain for a good harvest.

questions.question: Why did Lencho say the raindrops were like 'new coins'?
answer_steps: The rain promised a good harvest, which meant money.
So the big drops seemed like ten-cent pieces and the little ones like fives.

questions.question: How did the rain change? What happened to Lencho's fields?
answer_steps: A strong wind began to blow and very large hailstones fell with the rain.
The hail destroyed the corn completely; the field was white, as if covered with salt.

questions.question: What were Lencho's feelings when the hail stopped?
answer_steps: His soul was filled with sadness: his crop was totally destroyed.
He said a plague of locusts would have left more, and the family feared hunger.

questions.question: Who or what did Lencho have faith in? What did he do?
answer_steps: He had complete faith in God.
He wrote a letter to God asking for a hundred pesos and posted it.

questions.question: Who read the letter? What did the postmaster do then?
answer_steps: The postman found it and took it to the postmaster, who read it.
Moved by Lencho's faith, the postmaster collected money from employees and friends and sent it, signed 'God'.

questions.question: Was Lencho surprised to find a letter for him with money in it? What made him angry?
answer_steps: No, he was not surprised, so great was his confidence in God.
He was angry because he got only seventy pesos instead of a hundred.

questions.question: Who does Lencho have complete faith in? Which sentences in the story tell you this?
answer_steps: Lencho has complete faith in God.
'He had but one hope: help from God, whose eyes, as he had been instructed, see everything, even what is deep in one's conscience.'
He was not surprised to see the money: 'Such was his confidence.'

questions.question: Why does the postmaster send money to Lencho? Why does he sign the letter 'God'?
answer_steps: He admires Lencho's faith and wants to help a man in need.
He signs it 'God' so as not to shake the writer's faith in God and to make Lencho believe God answered him.

questions.question: Did Lencho try to find out who had sent the money to him? Why/Why not?
answer_steps: No, he did not.
He was sure that God had sent it; he had no doubt at all, so it never occurred to him that people might have helped him.

questions.question: Who does Lencho think has taken the rest of the money? What is the irony in the situation?
answer_steps: He thinks the post-office employees took the rest and calls them 'a bunch of crooks'.
The irony is that these very employees gave their own money to help him, and they are the ones he blames.

questions.question: Are there people like Lencho in the real world? What kind of a person would you say he is? (Choose from: greedy, naive, stupid, ungrateful, selfish, comical, unquestioning.)
answer_steps: Yes, many simple people have such strong faith.
Lencho is naive and unquestioning in his faith; he is also, without realising it, ungrateful to the people who helped him.
He is hard-working, not greedy: he asks only for what he needs.

questions.question: There are two kinds of conflict in the story: between humans and nature, and between humans themselves. How are these conflicts illustrated?
answer_steps: Humans vs nature: the hailstorm destroys Lencho's ripe corn completely.
Humans vs humans: Lencho distrusts the post-office employees and calls them crooks, though they helped him.

questions.question:
Read the extract and answer the questions.

*The air was fresh and sweet. The man went out for no other reason than to have the pleasure of feeling the rain on his body,*
*and when he returned he exclaimed, "These aren't raindrops falling from the sky, they are new coins.*
*The big drops are ten cent pieces and the little ones are fives."*

(i) Who is 'the man' in the extract?

(ii) Why did he go out?

(iii) Why does he call the raindrops 'new coins'?

(iv) Name the figure of speech in 'they are new coins'.

(v) What was his mood at this moment?
answer_steps: (i) Lencho, the farmer.
(ii) Just for the pleasure of feeling the rain on his body.
(iii) Rain promised a good harvest, which meant money.
(iv) Metaphor.
(v) Happy and hopeful.

questions.question:
Read the extract and answer the questions.

*The field was white, as if covered with salt.*
*Not a leaf remained on the trees. The corn was totally destroyed.*
*The flowers were gone from the plants. Lencho's soul was filled with sadness.*

(i) What made the field white?

(ii) Name the figure of speech in 'as if covered with salt'.

(iii) What happened to the corn?

(iv) How did Lencho feel?

(v) What did Lencho say a plague of locusts would have done?
answer_steps: (i) Hailstones.
(ii) Simile.
(iii) It was totally destroyed.
(iv) Full of sadness.
(v) It would have left more than this.

questions.question:
Read the extract and answer the questions.

*But later, struck by the faith of the man who wrote it, he decided to answer the letter.*
*But when he opened it, it was evident that to answer it he needed something more than goodwill, ink and paper.*
*But he stuck to his resolution: he asked for money from his employees, he himself gave part of his salary.*

(i) Who is 'he' in the extract?

(ii) What struck him about the letter?

(iii) What else did he need besides goodwill, ink and paper?

(iv) Give a word from the extract that means 'firm decision'.

(v) What quality of the postmaster does this show?
answer_steps: (i) The postmaster.
(ii) The faith of the man who wrote it.
(iii) Money.
(iv) Resolution.
(v) Kindness and generosity.

questions.question:
Read the extract and answer the questions.

*"God: Of the money that I asked for, only seventy pesos reached me. Send me the rest, since I need it very much.*
*But don't send it to me through the mail because the post office employees are a bunch of crooks. Lencho."*

(i) Who wrote this letter, and to whom?

(ii) How much money had he asked for?

(iii) Whom does he call 'a bunch of crooks'?

(iv) What does 'crooks' mean?

(v) What is ironic about this letter?
answer_steps: (i) Lencho wrote it to God.
(ii) A hundred pesos.
(iii) The post-office employees.
(iv) Dishonest people, cheats.
(v) The people he calls crooks are the ones who gave him the money.

questions.question: 'The field was white, as if covered with salt.' The figure of speech is:
questions.explanation: 'As if' introduces a comparison.
option_feedback: There is 'as if', so it is a direct comparison: a simile.

questions.question: 'They are new coins.' Here the raindrops are compared to coins. This is a:
questions.explanation: The drops are called coins directly.
option_feedback: It is a comparison, not an exaggeration.
There is no play on words.

questions.question: Where was Lencho's house?
options: on the bank of the sea
on the crest of a low hill in the valley
questions.explanation: It was the only house in the entire valley.
option_feedback: He went to town to post the letter.

questions.question: What did Lencho's field of corn need, according to him?
options: a downpour or at least a shower
questions.explanation: The ripe corn promised a good harvest if it rained.
option_feedback: His sons were working in the field.

questions.question: 'A plague of locusts would have left more than this.' Lencho means that:
options: the hail caused more damage than locusts would have
questions.explanation: Locusts eat crops; the hail was even worse.

questions.question: Why did Lencho write a letter to God?
options: to thank God for the rain
to ask for a new house
to ask for a hundred pesos to sow his field again and live until the next crop
questions.explanation: He believed God sees everything and would help.
option_feedback: He wrote the second letter about the employees.
He needed money for seed and food.

questions.question: How is the postmaster described?
questions.explanation: 'Amiable' means friendly.

questions.question: What did the postmaster first do on reading the letter?
options: he reported Lencho to the police
he laughed, but then became serious and admired the writer's faith
he sent it back to Lencho
questions.explanation: He was struck by the faith of the man who wrote it.
option_feedback: He kept it and answered it.

questions.question: How did the postmaster collect money for Lencho?
options: from his employees, his friends and part of his own salary
questions.explanation: It was an 'act of charity'.
option_feedback: Lencho's was the only house in the valley.

questions.question: How did Lencho react when he saw the money?
options: he was not surprised but became angry after counting it
he was shocked and thanked the postmaster
questions.explanation: His confidence in God was so great that he expected it.
option_feedback: He never knew who sent it.
He kept it and asked for more.

questions.question: Whom did Lencho call 'a bunch of crooks'?
questions.explanation: He thought they had taken thirty pesos.
option_feedback: He had no neighbours in the valley.
They are not in the story.

questions.question: The word 'amiable' means:
questions.explanation: The postmaster was an amiable, kind man.
option_feedback: It describes his nature, not his work.

questions.question: 'An ox of a man, working like an animal in the fields' describes Lencho as:
questions.explanation: He worked tirelessly on his land.

questions.question: Which word best describes Lencho's faith?
questions.explanation: He never questions God, even when he gets less money.

questions.question: What did Lencho write on the envelope?
questions.explanation: This made the postman laugh.

questions.question: On which day did Lencho go to the post office for his reply?
questions.explanation: He came a bit earlier than usual.

questions.question: The ending of the story is an example of:
questions.explanation: The outcome is the opposite of what one would expect.
option_feedback: It is about faith and kindness.
It is not a sad death.

questions.question: What helped the family on the sorrowful night after the storm?
options: their hope of help from God
questions.explanation: 'No one dies of hunger,' they said.

questions.question: Why did the postmaster call the reply 'an act of charity'?
options: because it was paid by the government
because the money was given freely to help someone in need
questions.explanation: It was given without expecting anything in return.

questions.question: What did Lencho do after counting the money?
options: he wrote another letter asking God for the rest
questions.explanation: He licked the stamp and pasted it with a blow of his fist.
option_feedback: He did not know about him.

questions.question: Which word in the story means 'the top of a hill'?
questions.explanation: 'The house was on the crest of a low hill.'

questions.question: The postmaster's action shows:
questions.explanation: He helped a stranger without any reward.

questions.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: The postmaster managed to send a full hundred pesos to Lencho.
questions.explanation: He could send only a little more than seventy pesos.
option_feedback: Not quite. He could send only a little more than seventy pesos.
Correct! He could send only a little more than seventy pesos.

questions.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: Lencho was surprised to receive the money.
questions.explanation: He was not surprised; such was his confidence in God.
option_feedback: Not quite. He was not surprised; such was his confidence in God.
Correct! He was not surprised; such was his confidence in God.

questions.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: The hailstorm lasted for about an hour.
questions.explanation: For an hour the hail rained on the house, garden, hillside and cornfield.
option_feedback: Correct! For an hour the hail rained on the house, garden, hillside and cornfield.
Not quite. For an hour the hail rained on the house, garden, hillside and cornfield.

questions.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: Lencho knew that the post-office employees had collected the money.
questions.explanation: He believed God sent it, and blamed the employees for the shortfall.
option_feedback: Not quite. He believed God sent it, and blamed the employees for the shortfall.
Correct! He believed God sent it, and blamed the employees for the shortfall.

questions.question: Describe the hailstorm and its effect on Lencho's field.
answer_steps: A strong wind blew and very large hailstones fell for an hour on the house, garden, hillside and cornfield.
The field became white, as if covered with salt; not a leaf was left and the corn was destroyed.
Lencho was filled with sadness.

questions.question: What kind of person was the postmaster? Give two reasons.
answer_steps: He was kind and generous: he gave part of his own salary.
He respected faith: he signed the letter 'God' so as not to shake Lencho's belief.

questions.question: Why did Lencho think the post-office employees were crooks?
answer_steps: He was sure God had sent the full hundred pesos.
When he got only seventy, he decided someone in the post office must have stolen the rest.

questions.question: 'Lencho was not surprised; such was his confidence.' Explain.
answer_steps: Lencho believed so completely in God that he expected the reply and the money.
So he felt no surprise, only anger when the amount was less.

questions.question: What did the family do on the night after the storm?
answer_steps: The night was sorrowful; they feared they would go hungry that year.
Their only hope was help from God: 'no one dies of hunger'.

questions.question: The postmaster and his employees showed true humanity. Do you agree? Explain with reference to the story.
answer_steps: Yes. The postmaster first laughed at a letter to God but was soon struck by the writer's faith.
Needing more than goodwill, ink and paper, he collected money from his employees and friends and gave part of his own salary.
He signed the reply 'God' so that Lencho's faith would not be shaken, and expected no thanks.
Even when Lencho called them crooks, their kindness remains: they helped a stranger out of pure goodwill.
Their humanity makes the ending ironic and touching.

questions.question: Write a character sketch of Lencho.
answer_steps: Lencho is a hard-working farmer, 'an ox of a man', who knows his fields and the weather.
He is hopeful: he calls raindrops new coins.
His faith in God is complete and unquestioning; after the hail he writes a letter to God for a hundred pesos.
He is naive: he never wonders who sent the money.
At the end he is unknowingly ungrateful, calling his helpers 'a bunch of crooks'.

answer_steps: Date and a heading; first-person voice.
Describe opening the second letter and reading that only seventy pesos reached him.
